title: Nuclei and Radioactivity
summary: A nucleus contains Z protons and N = A − Z neutrons. For example, O-18 has 8 protons (and 8 electrons) and 10 neutrons; U-238 has 92 protons and 146 neutrons.
Nuclear radius R = R₀A^⅓, with R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm, so all nuclei have roughly the same density.

Nuclear force: very strong, short-range (about 2–3 fm), charge-independent (it acts equally between n–n, p–p and n–p), attractive (repulsive at very short distances), saturating and non-central. It is the strongest force in nature; gravity is the weakest.
Mass defect and binding energy: Δm = [Zm_p + (A − Z)m_n] − M, and B.E. = Δm c². One atomic mass unit (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) is equivalent to 931 MeV (1.49 × 10⁻¹⁰ J).

Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of α, β or γ rays by unstable nuclei, discovered by Henri Becquerel in 1896. It is a nuclear process, so it is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination.

α-particle: a helium nucleus (+2e); it has the greatest ionizing power and the least penetration. β-particle: a fast electron (−e); intermediate on both counts. γ-rays: electromagnetic, uncharged; the most penetrating.

Displacement laws: α-decay lowers A by 4 and Z by 2 (U-238 → Th-234). β⁻-decay raises Z by 1 with A unchanged; the apparent breach of energy conservation in β-decay led Pauli to predict the neutrino. γ-decay changes neither A nor Z.
dN/dt = −λN, so N = N₀e^(−λt). Half-life T½ = 0.693/λ, and the mean life τ = 1/λ. The decay curve is exponential.
After n half-lives, N = N₀/2ⁿ: three half-lives leave ⅛ and four leave 1/16.
Examples: T½ = 8 days takes 24 days to fall to ⅛. Activity falling to ⅛ in 30 years means T½ = 10 years. Falling to 1/32 in 25 days means T½ = 5 days.
Activity A = λN is measured in becquerel (1 Bq = 1 decay/s); 1 curie = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq.

Bombarding nuclei with particles (α, p, n) changes one element into another — in principle even iron into gold. Rutherford (1919): N-14 + α → O-17 + p. The neutron is the best projectile because it is uncharged and is not repelled by the nucleus.
Moderators such as heavy water or graphite slow down neutrons in a reactor.

Calculate the energy equivalent to 1 atomic mass unit. (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
Mention four characteristics of nuclear force.

(1) It is the strongest force in nature. (2) It is short-range (about 2–3 fm). (3) It is charge-independent (n–n, p–p, n–p alike). (4) It saturates — each nucleon attracts only its neighbours; it is attractive except at very short distances.
sa: State the law of radioactive decay. Define half-life and decay constant and relate them. Draw the decay curve.

Law: the rate of decay is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei, dN/dt = −λN, giving N = N₀e^(−λt).
Decay constant λ: the fraction of nuclei decaying per unit time.
Half-life T½: the time for half the nuclei to decay. Setting N = N₀/2 gives T½ = ln 2/λ = 0.693/λ.
Curve: N against t falls exponentially — N₀, N₀/2, N₀/4 … at equal intervals of T½.
Compare α, β and γ radiations.

Nature: α — helium nuclei (+2e); β — electrons (−e); γ — electromagnetic waves (no charge).
Ionizing power: α greatest, γ least.
Penetrating power: α least (stopped by paper), β moderate (a few mm of aluminium), γ greatest (several cm of lead).
Effect on the nucleus: α lowers A by 4 and Z by 2; β raises Z by 1; γ changes neither.
la: What are mass defect and binding energy? Explain the main properties of the nuclear force.

Mass defect Δm = [Zm_p + (A − Z)m_n] − M_nucleus: the nucleus weighs less than its separate nucleons.
Binding energy = Δm c² (931 MeV per u): the energy needed to break the nucleus into its nucleons. Binding energy per nucleon measures stability; it is highest (about 8.8 MeV) near iron.
Nuclear force: (1) strongest force known; (2) very short range; (3) charge-independent; (4) saturating; (5) attractive except at very small distances, where it is repulsive; (6) it is what holds protons together against their electrostatic repulsion.
